source.title: Dissecting Geometric Constraints in Grokking: Interaction-Dependent Acceleration in Modular Arithmetic
source.authors: Zachary A. Hampton; Wasiq Khan; B. Khan

record.tranche_reason: Tests modular-arithmetic grokking outcomes under component and configuration changes, using held-out accuracy crossing times; it is not an explicit replication of the original recipe.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own test-accuracy crossing counts and times for modular-arithmetic models under factorial component settings, configuration comparisons, and task and depth sweeps. It does not report training-accuracy trajectories aligned to the crossings or vary training-set size. The authors' cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains small modular-arithmetic transformers and reports its own held-out accuracy crossing counts and times. It varies weight decay, projection, readout, logit scale, task, prime and depth. This bears on whether and when algorithmic grokking occurs (V1) and on the role of weight decay (V5). It never reports training-accuracy timing, so the delay after training saturation is not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that projection accelerated grokking in shallow modular transformers via interactions with readout and decay, but was neither sufficient nor required. Sphere+Fourier generalized earlier across five partitions, although fewer of its two-layer runs finished above threshold. Reliability also varied with task and depth.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular arithmetic and held-out accuracy crossing, but studies a different intervention recipe: a factorial of residual projection, readout normalization, logit scale, and weight decay, plus Sphere+Fourier configurations. The standard evaluation uses a 30/70 split and a first checkpoint above 0.95; it is not an explicit reproduction of the original source recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Crossing outcomes and times vary with projection, readout weight normalization, logit scale, weight decay, task, prime, depth, and configuration. The authors also note that the 200-epoch evaluation grid limits temporal resolution.

fits_no_version.finding: After first crossing, 22/25 two-layer baseline runs and 7/25 Sphere+Fourier runs later dropped to ≤0.95 test accuracy. Five Sphere+Fourier runs ended below threshold despite training accuracy 1.0 (Table S8, post hoc).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokked generalization in modular-arithmetic transformers is not always stable; relapses after first crossing are common under some configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Hard unit-norm residual projection with normalized readout cuts crossing time 8–37× relative to matched unprojected models (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural norm constraints on the residual stream can largely remove the grokking delay in modular arithmetic.

record.code_released: The repository is private; access is provided on demand.
record.problems: The evidence is limited to small modular-arithmetic transformers. The independent-partition study tests five partitions and five model seeds; the 200-epoch evaluation grid may miss brief changes; the persistence analysis was post hoc; and projection contrasts cannot separate geometry from output scale. Most factorial settings use one learning rate, prime, operation, and depth. No dataset-size sweep or aligned training-accuracy trajectory is reported for the crossing results.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted the individual logit-scale sweep (Supplementary Table S5), Fourier-frequency controls (Table S6), soft-penalty settings (Figure S1), detailed persistence counts and trajectories (Table S8 and Figure S2), token-embedding representation measurements (Table S9 and Figure S3), and duplicate summary rows for factorial contrasts and partition-level advantages. These report additional crossing, persistence, or representation details; the selected rows retain the main factorial, partition, task, depth, and normalization outcomes.

untested.parts: Delay relative to training-accuracy saturation; chance-level test accuracy before the jump; dependence of the delay on training-set size (split fixed at 30/70).
Circuit efficiency, any low-norm mechanism, critical dataset size, and ungrokking. Only the presence or absence of weight decay is varied.
No circuit or progress-measure analysis. The token-embedding dimensionality comparison is explicitly descriptive.
Only algorithmic data. No initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich manipulation.
Learned algorithms are not identified or compared.
No optimizer or floating-point artifact controls. AdamW is used throughout.

missing.what: Post hoc persistence and relapse counts, including relapses where training accuracy also fell
Logit-scale sweep with N=1, C=1, W=1: all crossed, and larger scales (50, 100) delayed crossing to 5,480–7,422 epochs
Soft norm-penalty runs: 0/80 crossings at any λ

record.verdict_notes: The study is a component dissection of an acceleration method, not a replication of Power et al. Its outcome is first test crossing >0.95 on a 200-epoch grid, and it lacks training-accuracy alignment, so the 'delay after training saturation' part of V1 is never directly measured. Fast Sphere+Fourier rows (~700 epochs) may reflect a bypassed delay rather than grokking in V1's sense. Several rows duplicate the same condition across tables (S2, S3, S4, S11). No row is a cited result.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary training-set size, so it does not test whether smaller training sets take longer to generalize. It does not report training-accuracy saturation alongside the test-accuracy crossings or establish that test accuracy remains at chance after training accuracy saturates.
No generalizing circuit, memorizing component removal, or continuous progress measure is tested. The token-embedding dimensionality comparison is described as descriptive and not causal.
The study uses algorithmic modular-arithmetic tasks only. It does not test non-algorithmic data, initialization scale, or a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.

Weight decay is varied and grokking outcomes are reported, but the study does not measure circuit efficiency, establish a low-norm mechanism, vary dataset size to find a critical size, or test ungrokking below such a size.
The study does not identify or compare learned algorithms across runs. It states that the factorial analysis did not identify the learned circuit.

The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts. Deterministic algorithms and a fixed hardware environment are reported, but no artifact-control comparison is made.

relationships.condition: Standard baseline (AdamW, weight decay 1) at depth ≥2 and across five partitions
